# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Atovaquone-driven DHODH restriction induces differentiation in oxidative cytarabine-residual AML

Hypothesis and premises. In oxidative cytarabine-residual AML retaining a differentiation block and inadequate pyrimidine salvage, atovaquone will restrict complex-III-supported DHODH before energetic collapse, inducing maturation and reducing leukemia propagation, conditional on the exposure gate below. Oxidative residual cells [S2] and DHODH-responsive AML [S4] are unmatched systems: their overlap and selective dependency are speculative. Residual disease is not assumed to be the ROS-low stem-cell population [S1][S2]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is an established comparator, not this repurposing proposal [S3].

Drug rationale and unverified premises. Unverified prior knowledge requiring independent checking is that atovaquone was originally approved to treat Pneumocystis pneumonia, is highly protein-bound, and can inhibit mammalian complex III. Also unverified here: DHODH requires oxidized ubiquinone; uridine bypasses de novo pyrimidine synthesis; brequinar inhibits human DHODH; and Saccharomyces cerevisiae Ura1 is a soluble, fumarate-dependent, respiratory-chain-independent DHODH. No Cmax, binding percentage, or potency numbers are verified by this packet; supplying confirmed numerical values would exceed its evidence. Selective pyrimidine restriction and normal-progenitor sparing remain assumptions.

Context qualification. Compare multiple primary cytarabine-pulse/washout residual specimens with matched untreated bulk AML and cycling-matched normal marrow progenitors. Proposed preregistered cutoffs—not validated biomarkers—are residual oxygen consumption per viable cell ≥1.5-fold matched untreated AML, <20% genotype-confirmed mature cells by morphology and a lineage-appropriate CD11b/CD14-containing panel, and ≤25% salvage contribution to UMP synthesis by isotope-resolved de novo/salvage flux partitioning at physiological uridine. Require persistent immaturity in vehicle controls. Record baseline dihydroorotate:orotate and uridine incorporation; incorporation alone is not the salvage-dependence gate. Biochemically validate brequinar, then test it in the same residual, bulk, and normal specimens. Residual samples advance only if it produces ≥2-fold dihydroorotate:orotate elevation, inadequate pool maintenance at physiological uridine, and ≥20-percentage-point genotype-confirmed maturation without substantial selective killing. Failure stops attribution of an atovaquone phenotype to this proposed context.

Exposure qualification. Before claiming clinical feasibility, independently verify approved-regimen total Cmax, free fraction, and exposure duration; calculate Cmax,u = Cmax,total × free fraction and confirm unbound exposure directly. Freeze the verified unbound ceiling without assuming dose escalation. Measure free drug in protein-containing culture media. Determine the free-drug EC50 for de novo pyrimidine-flux inhibition, accompanied by CoQ reduction and dihydroorotate:orotate elevation. An EC50 exceeding the clinical ceiling rejects exposure feasibility. Culture schedules must also respect verified exposure duration; plasma exposure alone cannot establish marrow exposure.

Mechanistic window and rescue. Across concentrations below that ceiling, sample at 0, 2, 6, 24, and 72 hours. Complex III inhibition/CoQ reduction and pyrimidine-flux suppression must precede maturation, with pool depletion occurring while ATP remains ≥80% of vehicle and excess apoptosis ≤10 percentage points. Pool depletion occurring only with ATP collapse stops interpretation and leaves the proposed selective window unsupported. Separate complex III assays from human-DHODH assays supplied with oxidized cofactor to distinguish indirect restriction from direct enzyme inhibition.

Use independently validated, nontoxic supraphysiological uridine supplementation and inducible cytosolic Ura1, expressed from 24 hours before dosing through the 72-hour endpoint. Confirm localization; include uridine-only and catalytically inactive-Ura1 controls; titrate expression to restore baseline pools without changing vehicle phenotype. Both rescues must restore pyrimidines and reverse brequinar-induced maturation and clonogenic loss; otherwise stop as uninterpretable. Under atovaquone, confirm that pyrimidine restoration leaves complex III inhibition and CoQ reduction intact.

Outcomes, alternatives, and falsification. Longitudinally track leukemia-genotype-confirmed cells, absolute viable counts, morphology, maturation markers, and post-washout clonogenicity. These distinguish differentiation from preferential immature-cell death or delayed cytarabine injury. Include vehicle, brequinar, and venetoclax–azacitidine [S3]. Only after these gates, extend to xenografts measuring marrow free exposure, secondary-transplant leukemia initiation, and normal hematopoietic recovery. Persistent maturation and propagation loss despite both validated rescues restoring pyrimidines falsifies the proposed DHODH-dependent mechanism. Bulk killing alone establishes neither differentiation nor stem-cell elimination.

Limitations and novelty. Physiological uridine, heterogeneous differentiation states, protein binding, and marrow distribution may eliminate the window. Comparable normal-progenitor colony or engraftment injury rejects selectivity; differentiation may not ensure durable control. Before claiming novelty, a mandatory prior-art search must identify any atovaquone-in-AML studies and distinguish this residual-cell CoQ–DHODH mechanism from existing OXPHOS-repurposing findings. Novelty remains unverified.

Ranked proposal:
Atovaquone-driven DHODH restriction induces differentiation in oxidative cytarabine-residual AML
